title: Remembering answers
objectives: Speed up a recursion with memoisation.
Cache with a dict or `functools.lru_cache`, keyed on hashable arguments
Spot a cache that serves stale answers

explain.text: Calls grow like the Fibonacci numbers themselves, by about 1.6 times per step. `fib(30)` makes 2,692,537 calls to compute 832,040. Only 31 different values are ever asked for.

screens.title: Keep a notebook
screens.prose: Now `fib` keeps a dict of answers. Before working, a call looks up its `n`; if the answer is stored, it returns it at once. Calls run left to right, so the left spine fills the dict first.
screens.question: Tap every call that finds its answer already stored.

hints.text: The left spine f(4), f(3), f(2), f(1), f(0) runs first and stores each value.
When this call runs, f(2) is already stored.
Each right-hand child arrives after its value was stored on the spine. So f(1) sits under f(3), f(2) under f(4) and f(3) under f(5).

feedback.correct: Three calls are answered from the dict, and their subtrees never run.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask, for each call, whether that value was stored before it ran.

byKey.a-a-a-a: This f(1) is the first f(1) to run, so it computes the value and stores it.
byKey.b-a: With the dict, this call never happens: its parent f(3) is answered from the dict.

explain.text: The three stored answers cut off their whole subtrees: 15 calls become 9, and each value is computed once. Storing answers to subproblems is called **memoisation**. It is top-down dynamic programming.

screens.title: Paths through a grid
screens.prose: A path moves right or down along the streets of a 3 by 4 grid of points. The last step into a point comes from above or from the left, so `paths(i, j) = paths(i - 1, j) + paths(i, j - 1)`.

state.caption: Paths from the top-left corner to each point, moving right or down

screens.question: How many paths reach the bottom-right point?

hints.text: First fill the point just left of the corner.
This point gets 3 from above and 3 from the left.
The left neighbour is $3 + 3 = 6$. The corner is $6 + 4 = 10$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the counts above and to the left, one point at a time.

byKey.row: That is the point left of the corner. The corner adds the 4 above it.
byKey.both: You may have added the corner's neighbours as 6 + 6. The point above the corner holds 4.

explain.text: Each point is the sum of the one above and the one to its left. Every path makes 2 down moves among 5, so there are $\binom{5}{2} = 10$. A memoised `paths` computes each point once.

screens.title: A stale price
screens.prose: A pricer caches discounted cash flows. Between calls the market moves and `rate` is updated.
screens.question: What does the program print?

options.why: You expected the cache to notice the new rate. It is keyed on `(100, 1)` only, so the second call returns the stored 95.24.
Floats and ints are hashable, so `lru_cache` stores them without trouble.
The first call runs while `rate` is still 0.05, and its result is stored.

hints.text: What does `lru_cache` use as the key for a stored result?
The second call has the same arguments as the first.
The key is `(100, 1)`. It was stored at 95.24, so the cache returns that without running the body.

feedback.correct: The cache returns a price computed at the old rate.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the arguments of the two calls.

byKey.fresh: You expected a new price at 10%. The cache key holds only the arguments, and they did not change, so the old 95.24 comes back.

explain.text: `price` reads `rate`, which is not one of its arguments. The cache cannot see it, so it serves the 5% price at 10%. Cache only pure functions: pass `rate` in as an argument.

screens.title: Top-down dynamic programming
screens.question: `value` is decorated with `@lru_cache`. Which call raises a `TypeError`?

options.why: A tuple of numbers is hashable, so it can be a cache key. Converting lists to tuples is the usual fix.
Floats are hashable. Only mutable containers such as lists, dicts and sets are not.
Strings are hashable, so they make good cache keys.

feedback.correct: A list is mutable, so it cannot be a dict key or a cache key.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which argument could change after being stored?

explain.text: `lru_cache` keeps a dict keyed by the arguments, and dict keys must be hashable. A list could change after it was stored, so Python refuses it. Pass `tuple(prices)` instead.

screens.title: Warm cache
screens.prose: A dict as a default argument is created once, when `def` runs, and shared by every call. Here `fib(5)` has already run.

params.title: Python
lines: cache[n] = n if n < 2 else fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2)

screens.question: How many `computing` lines does `fib(6)` print?

hints.text: Is `cache` empty when `fib(6)` starts?
These values are stored by the first call.
`cache` still holds 0 to 5. Only 6 is new, and its two lookups are hits.

feedback.correct: One line, `computing 6`: the default dict kept the earlier answers.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The default dict is not reset between calls.

byKey.fresh: You expected a new empty cache per call. A default argument is built once, so 0 to 5 are already stored.
byKey.none: 6 has never been asked for, so it must be computed once.

explain.text: The default dict outlives each call, so the first call after warm-up is mostly cache hits. That is harmless for pure `fib`, but a counter or a changed input makes it a surprise. A cache made inside the function, or by `lru_cache`, is clearer.

screens.title: Memoise two recursions
screens.prose: `fib_memo(n)` returns `(fib(n), computed)`, where `computed` counts the values worked out rather than read from the cache, base cases included. `grid_paths(r, c)` counts right-or-down paths across an $r \times c$ grid of points. Each call starts with an empty cache.
screens.question: Write `fib_memo(n)` and `grid_paths(r, c)` with a cache.

widget.how: Check runs 14 hidden tests. `computed` must match exactly; `fib_memo(10)` run twice must count 11 both times. `grid_paths(18, 18)` would take billions of calls without the cache, and one test compares with $\binom{r + c - 2}{r - 1}$.

hints.text: In `f`: return a cached value at once; otherwise add 1 to `computed`, work the value out, store it and return it.
A point on the top row or left column has exactly one path.
`paths(i, j)`: return 1 if `i == 1 or j == 1`; else cache `paths(i - 1, j) + paths(i, j - 1)` under the key `(i, j)`.

feedback.correct: Each subproblem is solved once, and the counts match.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 expects `(0, 1)`: `fib(0)` is computed once, as a base case. Count base cases too.
byKey.test-4: Test 4 expects 31. If you got 59, you counted cache lookups as well as computations.
byKey.test-6: Test 6 ran `fib_memo(10)` twice. A count other than 11 means the cache or counter outlived the first call.
byKey.test-12: Test 12 timed out or failed: memoise `paths` on the key `(i, j)`.

explain.text: Both functions solve each distinct state once: $n + 1$ values for `fib`, $r \times c$ points at most for the grid. The cache is made inside the call, so each call starts clean. The grid count equals $\binom{r + c - 2}{r - 1}$.

screens.title: A binomial pricer
screens.prose: An option is priced on a 30-step binomial tree. Up then down reaches the same price as down then up, so a node's value depends only on `(step, ups)`. A memoised `value(step, ups)` computes each node once.
screens.question: How many node values does the memoised pricer compute, from step 0 to step 30?

hints.text: Step $k$ has $k + 1$ distinct nodes. Add them up.
Step 30 alone has 31 nodes.

feedback.correct: 496 values, against about a billion paths.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the distinct nodes at each step, 0 to 30.

byKey.paths: That is the number of paths. Paths that recombine share a node, and the cache values each node once.
byKey.square: You used $31 \times 31$. Step $k$ has only $k + 1$ nodes, so the total is a triangle.
byKey.last: That is the final step only. Every earlier step's nodes are valued too.

explain.text: The tree recombines, so 30 steps have only 496 distinct nodes against $2^{30}$ paths. Memoising on `(step, ups)` is exactly the backward induction of a binomial pricer. The key holds everything the value depends on.

ideas: Naive recursion recomputes the same subproblems: `fib(30)` makes 2,692,537 calls for 31 different values.
Memoisation stores each answer the first time, so the work is the number of distinct states times the work per state. It is top-down dynamic programming.
A cache is only safe for a pure function with hashable arguments: anything the answer depends on must be in the key.

formula.name: Calls with and without a cache
formula.note: Naive calls grow like the Fibonacci numbers; memoised work grows like $n$.

summary.trap: Caching a function that reads something outside its arguments, such as a global rate or `self.rate`, returns stale answers.

quiz.prose: A calibration loop runs 200 passes. Each pass prices the same 25 bonds through a pure `price(yld, maturity)` wrapped in `lru_cache`.
quiz.question: How many prices are actually computed?

feedback.correct: 25: the first pass fills the cache, and the other 199 are lookups.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the distinct argument pairs.

byKey.all: You counted every call. After the first pass every call is a cache hit.

explain.text: Only 25 distinct keys ever appear, so 25 prices are computed. If the yields moved each pass, the keys would change and the cache would barely help.

quiz.question: What does it print?

options.why: You expected the cache to see the new rate. The key is `(c, 2)`, and `c` is the same object, so the old value returns.
Ordinary objects are hashable by identity, so `self` makes a valid key.

feedback.correct: The stale 5% value: the key ignores `self.rate`.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. What does the cache key hold?

explain.text: `lru_cache` keys on `self` by identity, not on its attributes. Changing `self.rate` leaves the key the same, so a stale factor comes back. The cache also keeps every `Curve` alive.

explain.text: Calls follow $C(n) = 1 + C(n-1) + C(n-2)$. So $C(7) = 1 + 25 + 15 = 41$, while memoised `fib(7)` computes 8 values.
